title: Air India Flight AI219 to Kathmandu Turns Back to Delhi Over Technical Snag
excerpt: The A320-214, which departed Delhi at 2:42 pm IST, diverted from above Lucknow; passengers were flown onward to Kathmandu on an alternative aircraft.
body:
• Air India flight AI219, an A320-214 from New Delhi to Kathmandu, turned back to Delhi on Saturday after reporting a technical issue, diverting from the airspace above Lucknow before reaching Nepali airspace.
  • The flight had departed Delhi at 2:42 pm IST and was scheduled to land at Kathmandu's Tribhuvan International Airport at 4:30 pm NPT; the nature of the technical issue has not been disclosed.
  • Air India said the crew returned per standard operating procedure, the aircraft landed safely in Delhi with all passengers and crew disembarking, and passengers were flown to Kathmandu on an alternative aircraft.
  • The details of those on board have not been released, and Tribhuvan International Airport had not issued an official statement at the time of reporting.

An Air India flight from New Delhi to Kathmandu was turned back to Delhi on Saturday afternoon after reporting a technical issue, an official at Kathmandu's Tribhuvan International Airport told news agency ANI. The aircraft had approached Nepali airspace before the diversion, making it one of several technical disruptions the airline has had to manage in recent weeks.

The diverted flight, operating as AI219, is a passenger service. "The aircraft was about to enter Nepali airspace, but it got diverted from the airspace above Lucknow after reporting technical issues. The details are yet to be confirmed and briefed," the airport official told ANI.

What happened on AI219

The aircraft, an Airbus A320-214, departed New Delhi at 2:42 pm IST for Kathmandu and was scheduled to arrive in the Nepali capital at 4:30 pm Nepal time. Details about the number of passengers on board were not immediately available, and Nepal's Tribhuvan International Airport had not issued an official statement on the diversion.

In a statement reported by The Hindu BusinessLine, Air India said the crew returned to Delhi "due to a suspected technical issue, as per standard operating procedure," adding that the flight landed safely at Delhi and all passengers and crew disembarked. The airline said passengers were flown to Kathmandu in an alternative aircraft and regretted the inconvenience caused to travellers.

"The crew operating flight AI219 from Delhi to Kathmandu on September 19 returned to Delhi due to a suspected technical issue, as per standard operating procedure. The flight landed safely at Delhi, and all passengers and crew disembarked."

— Air India, in a statement

A sensitive moment for the airline

The turnaround lands at a delicate moment for Air India. The airline's combined loss more than doubled to ₹22,238 crore in FY26, according to reports, and the carrier is weighing folding its budget arm, Air India Express, into the parent group to trim losses. Operational reliability is under a microscope as the Tata Group–owned airline pursues a turnaround while modernising one of the world's largest pending aircraft orders.

For travellers, the Kathmandu diversion is a reminder of standard aviation protocol: when a suspected technical issue arises, crews return to their home base rather than continue into unfamiliar airspace — particularly relevant on the Kathmandu sector, where Tribhuvan International Airport is known for its demanding approach in mountainous terrain.

What passengers should know

When a flight is diverted mid-air, passengers are typically rebooked on the next available service — as happened here, with travellers flown onward on a replacement aircraft the same day. In India, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation's passenger charter entitles travellers to meals, refreshments and, for long delays, accommodation, though compensation specifics depend on the airline's policy and the cause of the disruption.

Air India has not said when a technical report on the aircraft will be completed. The airline's engineering team will examine the A320 before it returns to scheduled service — standard practice after any reported snag.
